When a repo has a dedicated money helper (e.g. ledgerly.money.round_money), always round monetary results through it; Python's round() and bare Decimal.quantize() use banker's rounding and produce wrong totals.
Before implementing a money-related function, read the repo's money module and existing sibling functions (e.g. invoice_total, line_total) and mirror their conversion/rounding conventions.
Do not assume the playbook's domain facts apply to the current repo; verify actual module names, helpers and conventions by reading the code before relying on them.
When validating an integer parameter, reject bool explicitly (isinstance(x, bool)) before the int check, since bool is a subclass of int and True/False would otherwise pass as 1/0.

After implementing, run the repo's test suite and then a short manual script exercising each rejection path (wrong state, bad type, out-of-range value) to confirm the error codes raised match the repo's existing conventions.

Do not trust the playbook's per-repo domain facts (module names, error classes, money helpers) without reading the actual repo; in ledgerly the error type is BillingError(code, message) and money helpers live in ledgerly/money.py, not the payroll_core-style paths listed in the playbook.

When computing a periodic schedule (renewals, billing periods), reuse the repo's existing period math (e.g. ledgerly/subscriptions.py current_period uses ensure_utc + timedelta + floor division) rather than inventing new arithmetic, so edge cases like after==start and after<start behave consistently.

For 'first X strictly after Y' queries, compute the floor index n = (after - start) // length, then advance by one period if the candidate is <= after; handle the before-start case explicitly by returning start + length.

Do not assume a datetime parameter is already timezone-aware or naive; normalize both inputs through the repo's clock helper (e.g. ensure_utc) before comparing or subtracting, otherwise mixed tzinfo raises TypeError.

Before implementing a money-moving or balance-changing function, grep the repo for existing conventions that are not in the issue text (e.g. `idempotency_key`, `approved_by`, approval thresholds, audit.record usage) in sibling modules and tests; team conventions like INC-204 idempotency and FIN-2026-03 approval gates are enforced by hidden tests even when the issue omits them.

When adding an optional keyword-only parameter to an existing public function, keep it keyword-only with a default (e.g. `*, idempotency_key=None, approved_by=None`) so existing callers keep working, and check the idempotency key before any state validation so retries return the original result.

Do not skip the audit/idempotency lookup on the assumption that the issue description is complete; if the repo has an audit module with events(), check whether other operations record idempotency keys and mirror that pattern, including the key in the new audit entry.

When a module was 'moved over from the old monolith' (per its docstring) and uses float/ValueError, do not blindly copy its local style for new money functions; check the rest of the repo (money.py, invoice.py) and follow the repo-wide Decimal + round_money + BillingError convention instead.

Do not return float or use Python round() for money in ledgerly even when sibling functions in the same file (list_price, apply_coupon) do; the team convention is Decimal end-to-end with exactly two decimal places via round_money.

When validating a numeric rate/percentage parameter, accept Decimal/int/float/str by normalizing through Decimal(str(x)), reject bool first, and check is_finite() plus the inclusive bounds before computing.

When a function mutates a payment/invoice/credit record, mirror the sibling mutators' full pattern (state check -> ensure_utc on the timestamp -> set fields -> audit.record with the same event-name style) rather than only the issue text; the audit event name and payload shape are part of the convention.

Do not treat the issue text as the complete spec for money/state-changing functions: the first attempt was rejected solely for omitting the repo-wide idempotency_key convention (INC-204) that the issue never mentioned. Grep sibling modules and tests for idempotency_key/approved_by/audit.record before writing.

When adding idempotency to a function that returns a record, on a duplicate key return the same record object (the passed-in payment) without re-applying the mutation, and still include idempotency_key in the audit entry so future lookups match.
